[[File:Cycle decomposition.svg|thumb|upright=0.75|A '''cycle decomposition''' of a graph. The edges are partitioned into two sets (blue and orange) where each set forms a [[Cycle (graph theory)|cycle]].]]

{{For|the notation used to express [[permutation]]s|Cycle decomposition (group theory)}}

In [[graph theory]], a '''cycle decomposition''' is a decomposition (a [[partition of a set|partitioning]] of a graph's edges) into [[Cycle (graph theory)|cycles]]. Every vertex in a graph that has a cycle decomposition must have even degree.

==Cycle decomposition of ''K<sub>n</sub>'' and ''K<sub>n</sub>'' − ''I''==
[[Brian Alspach]] and Heather Gavlas established necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a decomposition of a [[complete graph]] of even order minus a [[Graph factorization|1-factor]] (a [[perfect matching]]) into even cycles and a complete graph of odd order into odd cycles.<ref>{{cite journal| doi=10.1006/jctb.2000.1996 | volume=81 | title=Cycle Decompositions of <math>K_n</math> and <math>K_n{-}I</math>&thinsp; | year=2001 | journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B | pages=77–99 | last1 = Alspach | first1 = Brian| doi-access=free }}</ref> Their proof relies on [[Cayley graph | Cayley graphs]], in particular, [[circulant graph |circulant graphs]], and many of their decompositions come from the action of a [[permutation]] on a fixed subgraph.

They proved that for positive even integers <math>m</math> and <math>n</math> with <math>4\leq m\leq n </math>, the graph <math>K_n-I</math> (where <math>I</math> is a 1-factor) can be decomposed into cycles of length <math>m</math> if and only if the number of edges in <math>K_n-I</math> is a multiple of <math>m</math>. Also, for positive odd integers <math>m</math> and <math>n</math> with <math>3\leq m\leq n</math>, the graph <math>K_n</math> can be decomposed into cycles of length <math>m</math> if and only if the number of edges in <math>K_n</math> is a multiple of <math>m</math>.

==Computational complexity==
The problem of decomposing an [[Eulerian graph]] into a minimum number of edge-disjoint cycles is [[NP-complete]], as is the corresponding problem of decomposing into a maximum number of cycles.<ref name="HeinrichStreicher2019">{{cite journal |last1=Heinrich |first1=Irene |last2=Streicher |first2=Manuel |title=Cycle decompositions and constructive characterizations |journal=Electronic Journal of Graph Theory and Applications |year=2019 |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=411–428 |doi=10.5614/ejgta.2019.7.2.15 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

An Eulerian graph has a unique number of cycles in all of its cycle decompositions if and only if no two edge-disjoint cycles in the graph share more than two vertices. This property can be decided in polynomial time: there exists an algorithm running in time <math>\mathcal{O}(n(n+m))</math> that determines whether the cycle number of a given Eulerian graph is unique, where <math>n</math> is the number of vertices and <math>m</math> is the number of edges.<ref name="HeinrichStreicher2019" />

==Algorithms==
Several approaches have been developed for finding optimal cycle decompositions. For the Maximum Eulerian Cycle Decomposition problem, [[column generation]] techniques can be applied to an [[integer linear programming]] model with an exponential number of variables.<ref name="Pinheiro2021">{{cite conference |last1=Pinheiro |first1=Pedro Olímpio |last2=Alexandrino |first2=Alexsandro Oliveira |last3=Oliveira |first3=Andre Rodrigues |last4=de Souza |first4=Cid Carvalho |last5=Dias |first5=Zanoni |title=Algorithms for the Maximum Eulerian Cycle Decomposition Problem |conference=LIII Simpósio Brasileiro de Pesquisa Operacional |year=2021 |location=João Pessoa, Brazil |url=https://www.ic.unicamp.br/~ra192804/SBPO_2021.pdf}}</ref>

[[Heuristic (computer science)|Heuristic approaches]] include [[greedy algorithm]]s that iteratively find minimum-sized cycles starting from random vertices, and '''ILP-based heuristics''' that solve restricted versions of the integer programming model using only a subset of possible cycles. These methods provide practical solutions for large instances where exact algorithms become computationally infeasible.<ref name="Pinheiro2021" />

==Applications==
===Network analysis===
Cycle decompositions can be applied to [[Markov chain|Markov processes]] on finite state spaces for analyzing [[directed graph|directed networks]]. Given an ergodic Markov chain with transition matrix <math>P</math> and stationary distribution <math>\pi</math>, the probability flow can be decomposed into cycles with positive weights. A stochastic decomposition approach yields a unique cycle decomposition where the weight <math>w(\gamma)</math> of each cycle <math>\gamma</math> equals the mean number of times a random walk passes through that cycle per time step.<ref name="DjurdjevacConrad2015">{{cite journal |last1=Djurdjevac Conrad |first1=Nataša |last2=Banisch |first2=Ralf |last3=Schütte |first3=Christof |title=Modularity of directed networks: Cycle decomposition approach |journal=Journal of Computational Dynamics |year=2015 |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=1–24 |doi=10.3934/jcd.2015.2.1 |arxiv=1407.8039}}</ref>

This approach can reveal modular structures in directed networks based on information flow rather than link density alone, providing insights that traditional methods may miss.<ref name="DjurdjevacConrad2015" />

===Genome rearrangement===
In [[comparative genomics]], cycle decompositions of [[breakpoint graph]]s are used to compute genome rearrangement distances. The Maximum Breakpoint Graph Decomposition problem can be reduced to the Maximum Eulerian Cycle Decomposition problem in polynomial time.<ref name="Pinheiro2021" />
